segments.title: Why don't governments encourage more history study?
segments.body: The conspiracy theory says governments dislike citizens studying history because researchers ask awkward questions. That explanation is rejected in favour of a seemingly efficient policy idea dating from about 2000. A government seeking value for money measures degrees by whether graduates enter directly related jobs. History's research and analytical skills can be used in other careers, so this question makes its value easy to underestimate. The resulting preference for STEM gives governments a quick answer to a complicated problem.

evidence.note: He raises and rejects the conspiracy explanation before turning to government efficiency.

The answer links direct degree-to-career surveys to STEM promotion, explains the transferable skills of history and humanities, and concludes that governments favour quick answers to complex problems.

segments.summary: The suggestion that governments fear politically awkward historical research is rejected. Institutional incentives and a seemingly efficient policy idea offer the main explanation.
segments.question: If history is so useful, why don't governments encourage people to study it more?
segments.answerShort: Measuring degrees by how directly they lead to related jobs favours STEM and can undervalue history's transferable research and analytical skills. It gives governments a quick policy answer to a complicated problem.

segments.title: The degree-to-job metric favours STEM
segments.body: The policy aims to get the greatest educational value for public money. Surveys ask how many graduates enter careers directly related to their degree, producing a clear and easily compared figure. Science, technology, engineering, and mathematics score well under that definition. The argument accepts that these are good degrees. The operative word is directly: the metric rewards subjects with a close path from degree to occupation.

evidence.note: He explains the survey question about careers directly related to a degree and why STEM scores highly.

segments.summary: When governments measure value by whether graduates work in jobs directly related to their degree, STEM subjects score strongly.

segments.title: History and humanities teach transferable skills
segments.body: History, arts, and humanities degrees often teach skills that do not point toward a single profession. Analysis and research can be applied in many fields, so graduates need not become professional historians for the degree to matter in their working lives. Few students in the teaching example become professional historians. The hope is that they will still share their passion for history and perhaps write a book. This helps explain why a direct degree-to-job comparison undervalues these subjects.

evidence.note: He describes history and humanities as transferable analysis and research skill sets rather than direct pipelines to historical careers.

segments.summary: History and humanities qualifications develop research and analytical skills that graduates can use in many professions.

segments.title: A simple metric produces a STEM-first policy answer
segments.body: Once the direct-career survey becomes the governing question, history and humanities can appear less valuable than STEM. The policy response then looks straightforward: de-emphasise those degrees and promote subjects that score better. The problem is that the simple survey result turns into an equally simple policy answer. In this account, modern politics favours quick and clear answers even when the underlying problem is more complicated than the chosen metric allows.

evidence.note: He links the survey result to pushing STEM and calls it a quick answer to a complex political problem.

segments.summary: A narrow employment measure can make history and humanities appear less valuable, leading governments to promote STEM as a simple answer to a complicated problem.
